principles.text: Make something people want. Nearly every startup death traces back to not doing that.
Don't try to think up startup ideas. Notice problems, preferably ones you have yourself.
Launch fast and measure weekly growth rate: 5-7% a week is good, 10% is exceptional.
Do things that don't scale: recruit early users by hand and make being your user great.
Determination matters more than intelligence. Good founders are relentlessly resourceful.

sampleQA.question: How do I know if my startup is growing fast enough?

answer.text: Measure growth as a weekly rate. During YC, 5-7% a week is good, 10% is exceptional, and 1% means you haven't figured it out yet.
Track the ratio of new customers to existing ones, not the absolute count. Small numbers compound if the rate holds.
Pick a target rate and hit it every week; anything that gets you that growth is the right thing to do.
After 8-9 months, check whether you're default alive: at current growth and expenses, do you reach profitability on the money left?

sampleQA.question: When and how should I raise a seed round?

answer.text: Raise when you can convince investors, not when you need money or hit an artificial deadline like Demo Day.
Talk to investors in parallel, ranked by expected value, and treat every investor as a no until they make a definite offer.
Assume deals will fall through, fit meetings around development, and take a reasonable offer from a reputable investor.
Act as if each raise is your last. The less you need more money, the easier it is to get.

sampleQA.question: Should I worry that competitors will copy my idea?

answer.text: In 99% of startups, failing to execute is a much bigger danger than being copied.
Far more startups die from poor execution by their founders than are killed by competitors.
Fear self-inflicted wounds: internal disputes, inertia, and above all ignoring users.
Nearly all ideas are easy to duplicate at first. Their value is the other ideas they lead to.
